newsitem.title: UK: Sluggish UK manufacturing sharpens BOE's dilemma.
newsitem.headline: Sluggish UK manufacturing sharpens BOE's dilemma.

text.p: Further evidence of slowing growth in Britain's sluggish manufacturing economy -- in stark contrast to lively activity in the services sector -- sharpens the dilemma for the Bank of England which meets next week to discuss the level of interest rates.

The July purchasing managers survey showed the manufacturing economy expanded for the 14th month in succession, but the pace of growth eased slightly as export orders fell for the first time since January 1996.

Many economists now expect slower growth in manufacturing may soon infect the healthy services sector and reduce the need for sharp interest rate rises this year, although it may not be enough to prevent a quarter point rate rise next week.
"The weakness in the manufacturing sector will continue and spread elsewhere in the economy," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.
"That in turn should negate the need for aggressive interest rate rises, although it will not be enough to stop a rise at next week's monetary policy committee meeting."
The rampant pound -- up around 25 percent on a trade-weighed basis since last August -- is punishing British manufacturers.

Firms depend heavily on export markets and around half British manufactured goods are sold abroad. They fear another interest rate rise will send sterling even higher, making their goods even more expensive overseas.
But all the signs from the central bank are that it will not allow the exchange rate to dictate policy and many economists expect a rate rise next week.

A Reuter poll conducted this week found 16 out of 23 London-based economists expect the Bank's monetary policy committee will put manufacturers' problems to one side and raise interest rates by a quarter point to 7.0 percent on August 7.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC markets, said the latest PMI survey makes grim reading for manufacturers.
"While it shows the pound's strength is hurting, the report is not weak enough to prevent the Bank of England from pushing up interest rates further to dampen consumer spending."
But the strong pound also means the outlook for inflation is improving, which should in turn mean less need to push rates up very sharply.

The PMI showed input prices sunk in July. The seasonally-adjusted prices index fell to 38.8 from 43.6 in June, the lowest level since the survey began in July 1991. Any reading below 50 represents a fall.
"Sterling's strength is not all bad news for industry. The further appreciation over the last month or so has intensified the downward pressure on firms' raw material costs," said Loynes.
"This bodes well for the inflation outlook and is likely to be echoed by the official producer prices figures for July."
But there were worrying signs from the survey that firms are starting to lay off staff in response to falling export orders.
The employment balance fell back to 51.0 from 52.3 in June.

"The rate of growth (of employment) recorded was slower than in previous months as an increasing number of firms were found to have cut employment levels as a direct result of weak export orders slowing demand," the survey said.
Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Securities, said there is a risk that the manufacturing sector could slip into recession next year if the Bank continues to raise rates.
"Further monetary tightening and sterling appreciation would increase fears that this sector will dip into recession in 1998," he said.
